en: A badger cub whose white stripe glows like a banked coal. It digs warm dens in meadow banks and naps in them through the heat of the day.
It tunnels through old charcoal pits, coming up grey with soot. The embers along its back flare when it is cross.
Its claws are hammered hard by digging through hot stone. Folk once followed its trails to find good iron.
It sits very still by its den and reads the smoke. The stripe on its face burns pale, like a lantern turned low.
A dormouse no bigger than a hazelnut, which it often hugs. It is gone at the first loud footstep.
It weaves a hedge of briars round its nest each autumn. Bramble seeds caught in its fur sprout where it sleeps.
It burrows down among old roots and wakes with stones grown into its coat. Its dens hold the soil of a whole hillside in place.
It sleeps through the cold with frost on its whiskers, and the frost does not melt when it wakes. Its breath leaves rime on the leaves.
A beaver kit that stacks twigs wherever it goes, whether or not there is any water to dam. It is very proud of each pile.
One night's work by a Dambrook can turn a trickle into a pond. Reedwood's marsh is said to be its handiwork.
Moss and reeds grow over its back until it looks like part of the dam it sleeps in. Marsh life gathers wherever it settles.
It left the rivers for the sea and swims through surf with a tail like a rudder. It slaps the waves to call its kin.
